overview: Tiwanaku was a major highland city near Lake Titicaca and the center of far-reaching religious and political connections during the first millennium CE. Its communities also settled lower valleys. “Tiahuanaco” is an older spelling. The broad imported outline is not proof of uniform imperial control, and its 1279 endpoint substantially outlasts the city’s main occupation.

periods.title: A highland center and regional connections
periods.summary: Monumental Tiwanaku flourished while agricultural communities extended into lower valleys.

periods.title: Urban dispersal
periods.summary: Recent dating places the city’s rapid loss of permanent residents in the early eleventh century; other communities followed different trajectories.

sections.title: Building a city high in the Andes

items.text: At roughly 3,850 meters above sea level, Tiwanaku stood in a demanding highland environment. Most buildings were made of earth, while major ceremonial structures used stone. The spectacular monuments are only the visible fraction of a much larger lived-in settlement.

Akapana had seven terraced levels and an internal drainage system. Managing rainwater mattered even in monumental ceremonial architecture. Carefully built channels helped water leave the structure instead of simply soaking through it.

Pumapunku masons shaped andesite blocks with precise recesses and finished details before assembly. Small holes helped workers grip and position some blocks. Their achievement becomes more impressive when studied as skilled human work, with identifiable building techniques.

Modern researchers have made small three-dimensional models of the scattered Pumapunku stones to test how they fit. Reassembly is difficult because many pieces were removed or broken after abandonment. A convincing model must work with the surviving blocks, rather than an imagined perfect temple.

Residential compounds grouped smaller buildings around open patios. Stone foundations helped protect adobe walls from rising moisture. Excavated cooking and storage pottery, bone tools and food remains recover the ordinary work that kept households going beside the famous monuments.

Some Tiwanaku homes incorporated burials beneath living areas. The placement brought certain dead relatives or ancestors into the spaces used by later residents. Archaeologists therefore study domestic buildings as places of family memory as well as cooking and sleeping.

Food remains vary among neighborhoods. Quinoa was widespread, with tubers and maize also present. Maize was not confined to the grandest residences: its differing distribution suggests that household connections and access mattered alongside social rank.

At Cerro San Antonio in Peru’s Locumba Valley, plant remains show that Tiwanaku settlers retained familiar highland foods, including quinoa and related plants, in a lower-altitude setting. Moving house did not mean forgetting what tasted like home.

Raised fields around Lake Titicaca placed crops on elevated beds separated by channels. Erickson’s research emphasizes that such systems could be built and maintained in manageable local units. Their scale does not by itself prove that a ruler commanded every farming household.

Keros were flaring cups used for chicha, a fermented corn drink, at ceremonies and everyday gatherings. They could be made from wood, clay or precious metal. Sharing drinks helped sustain relationships; the container could also advertise its owner’s standing.

One wooden kero, dated 500 to 1000 CE, carries four winged staff-holding figures carved around its surface. Two have feline faces and two have bird-of-prey heads. The cup turns in the hand like a small gallery of powerful beings.

No securely readable Tiwanaku sentence survives for an original-language sample and translation. Carved figures on monuments and vessels carried meaning, but they are not a deciphered written text. Even applying the later name Viracocha to Tiwanaku’s central staff-bearing figure remains uncertain.

ending.text: A 2023 radiocarbon study places rapid urban collapse around 1010 to 1050 CE, before the later drought often blamed for it. This finding concerns Tiwanaku itself: traditions continued in other communities, and visitors returned afterward. Its urban institutions changed dramatically, but its people did not vanish. The imported 1279 map endpoint is not a supported collapse date.
